The countries who learned less than their parents wont have a great economy because it will be harder for them to get a good job.

raw_comment:
#1 South Korea has the highest upward mobility, while Czech Republic has the least upward mobility and the most amount of children getting the same amount of education than their parents.  I believe this effects the jobs they get, and the amount of money they get in return for their job. In short, a better education gives you a better job, which then gets you a better income; and the opposite can happen as well.

#2 I believe this way of calculating the educational differences is amazing, it gives a great estimate of if the majority of the population’s education is getting better or worse.

#3 The amount of upwardly mobile just barely beats out downwardly mobile, and the amount for the same education is more than upwardly mobile and downwardly mobile combined. The state of the country isn’t bad or concerning, but it’s not good either. It does make a lot of sense though in the state of the country.
#4 Maybe less industrial jobs would help, or less physical activities available to them.

Which country has the greatest upward mobility?  Which has the least?  Which country has the most children with about the same education level as their parents.  How do you think this degree of education mobility has affected these countries economically and socially?
 
South Korea has the highest upward mobility. Czech Repeplic has the least upward mobility. Czech Repeblics students have the most same education level as their parents. I'm not sure how it effects.
 
 
 
Describe the education mobility for children in your country using these graphs.
 
Most children have equal educational mobility as their parents in our country.
	
 
In the United States, the percentage of women with post-high school education is about 25 percent greater than men.  How would you explain this?  What changes do you think might increase the men’s  percentage?
 
	Mostly women are motivated to get into college in my opinion. If the men were as motivated.
 
— What do you think of this method of calculating educational mobility — comparing a child to the highest educational achievement by a parent?
I think this is an effective method.

South Korea has the highest upward mobility and the Czech republic has the least upward mobility. The Czech republic has similar school. South Korea has the best school.
 
 — What do you think of this method of calculating educational mobility — comparing a child to the highest educational achievement by a parent?

I think that this method is really useful.

Most children have the same education as their parents in are country.

Mostly women like to get more education and are more serious and like money. The men would percentage would increase if they are more motivated.

Thanks to all students who responded.  Love the catchy headlines that capture the main ideas of the map:  “The Numbers Don't Lie, the Girls are Schooling the Boys” by Claire of Andover, “Who Knows More?” by Devlyn of NJ, and “World of Women: An International Educational Trend” by Mr. Card’s A Block. 

I would like to make particular mention of Jiyoung of US who replied to Megan of HHHS. (Control F for “Jiyoung” to find the reply.) As a Korean living in the US, she explained why South Korea has such a high level of educational success.  It has to do with Korean history and culture.  Thank you for sharing your perspective.  We hope others will follow his example.

You can continue to post responses.  Please check back tomorrow --  Thursday afternoon, OCTOBER 3 to see the Reveal with a link to the original New York Times article, some questions about the graphs, and some Stat Nuggets.
 The next graph will be released tomorrow -- THURSDAY, OCTOBER 3, with moderation on WEDNESDAY, OCTOBER 9.  You may respond before, during, or after the live moderation by going to ““What's Going On In This Graph?”  The topic --  global temperatures.  

Also, you can view the webinar with teachers and students discussing how to learn from graphs using The New York Times.  Go tohttps://webinars.on24.com/nyt/Graphs?partnerref=OnDemand.

raw_comment: These graphs show differences in education between people and their parents, men and women, and different nations. The graph on the left shows what percent of people who got more, the same, or less education than their parents. The graph shows that South Korea had the highest percentage of people who received more education than their parents, and the United States was on the lower end of the scale. I wonder why the United States is so low on the graph. I also wonder why South Korean education has allowed so many people to receive more education than their parents. The graph on the right shows the percentage of men and women who received secondary education after high school. In every country studied, women had a higher percentage of secondary education than men. I wonder why so many more women are receiving secondary education, and if this correlates with the percent of women with jobs. One possible title for this graph is "Education Across the World".

raw_comment:
Headline: Education on the Rise

I noticed that the date on this graph is from 2012. I also noticed that more women had further education after college. South Korea obtained the largest amount of people to go to school after high school. South Korea really seems to be on the rise with their education, considering that the majority of the people are receiving more education than their parents did. The US is surprisingly not as high as I thought it would be, but maybe the statistics have changed since 2012 and 2014. In the dotted graph for the US, more women also seek further education than men do.

I wonder why they used data from 2012. How much has education changed since 2012? Why is the Czech Republic education on the downfall? What leads to a decrease in education in some countries?

raw_comment:
In South Korea, there is more pressure for students to go into higher education. They are told that the only way to get a good job is to go to the best universities. Even after their school days, they spend hours at cram schools trying to improve their test scores. This factor could explain the graph on the left because students face an overbearing amount of pressure to make more money than their parents.  That begs the question, how much of a role does money play into young adults pursuing higher education? And what role does the government play in getting more people to pursue higher education? For example, in Denmark, the country pays for students to pursue higher education. This is kind of confusing because why is Denmark lower on the list. It also makes me question, what kind of social pressures are put on students from countries closer to the top of the graph to pursue higher education to their parents?
For the graph on the right, it looks like it is exemplifying the shift from men to women pursuing higher education. This might question if women are pursuing higher(college) education because of gender discrimination in thee workplace?

raw_comment:
Headline: Education on the Rise

I noticed that the date on this graph is from 2012. I also noticed that more women had further education after college. South Korea obtained the largest amount of people to go to school after high school. South Korea really seems to be on the rise with their education, considering that the majority of the people are receiving more education than their parents did. The US is surprisingly not as high as I thought it would be, but maybe the statistics have changed since 2012 and 2014. In the dotted graph for the US, more women also seek further education than men do.

I wonder why they used data from 2012. How much has education changed since 2012? Why is the Czech Republic education on the downfall? What leads to a decrease in education in some countries?

raw_comment:
In South Korea, there is more pressure for students to go into higher education. They are told that the only way to get a good job is to go to the best universities. Even after their school days, they spend hours at cram schools trying to improve their test scores. This factor could explain the graph on the left because students face an overbearing amount of pressure to make more money than their parents.  That begs the question, how much of a role does money play into young adults pursuing higher education? And what role does the government play in getting more people to pursue higher education? For example, in Denmark, the country pays for students to pursue higher education. This is kind of confusing because why is Denmark lower on the list. It also makes me question, what kind of social pressures are put on students from countries closer to the top of the graph to pursue higher education to their parents?
For the graph on the right, it looks like it is exemplifying the shift from men to women pursuing higher education. This might question if women are pursuing higher(college) education because of gender discrimination in thee workplace?

raw_comment: Students in South Korea and southeast Asia, in general, feel more pressure to pursue a higher education. On the right graph, it is clear that the percentage of women in every country are pursuing a higher education than men. Does maturity play a large role in this data? Cost for higher education varies country to country- does this also play a large role? Do people in countries with a low cost higher education have more incentive to go to college? Also, the status quo must vary per family per country. If your parents went to college and you went to college, you received the same level of education. On the other hand, if your parents only completed a limited education (middle school, rather than high school or college) and you got a college education, you are part of the upwardly mobile trend. At some point, if everyone receives a higher education as do their parents, the status quo section will increase until the entire graph is the same or less, rather than a ix of all 3. I think this is why Italy is so high on the left graph, and so low on the right one; students may be doing better than their parents, but not at a level higher than high school.

Welcome to Wednesday's live moderation of  “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  I am moderating with Nick Simonetti from West Guilford High School, South Carolina.

Today’s release has a segmented bar graph and a chart that shows how selected countries compare regarding education mobility.  Notice how the education attainment of young adults compares to their parents. Wonder how this relates to the percentage of people who have gone onto education beyond high school.  

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?", and  "What's going on in this graph?"  

Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas about the graph. 

On Thursday afternoon, we’ll reveal the article that included this graph and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.

The next “What’s Going On in This Graph?” will be released tomorrow -- Thursday, OCTOBER 3 with moderation on Wednesday, OCTOBER 9.  The topic – global temperatures.

This could be because men are stricter with who they bring in to the workforce, so women won't get a chance to do what they want so they go to the education side. Could it be college, community college, or could trade school fall into that category?

raw_comment:
I noticed that it seems the majority of people in 2012 received the same level of education as their parents did. Something that contributes to this is it is easier for children to follow in their parent's footsteps than it is for them to forge their own path unless they are being supported to do so by their parents. 

I also noticed, like a lot of people, that women are on the rise in higher education. An issue that may be attributed to this may be the gendered stereotyping that takes place in the work place. Women in the majority of workplaces are less likely to be hired than a male of the same qualifications. In today's age of social improvement, a lot of auditions or interviews are conducted in such a manor that gender discrimination cannot occur. However, the gender blind cannot always happen. This is why women are on the rise in higher education, because they have to seek out more qualifications to obtain a job in the modern work force. 

I wonder what would happen to the data if a segment including standardized testing would be added to the table. What countries would be on top then? 

The headline might go along the lines of "Women on the rise, seeking out higher education"

raw_comment:
I notice that South Korea is thriving in higher education and has an upwardly mobile percentage of people getting a higher education than their parents while we in the US have more of a status quo percentage. I also notice that females are excelling in education in every single country on the graph. I wonder why it is that South Korea is flourishing in education in comparison to the US. Could it be that the recent economic boom in South Korea is what is inspiring all these students to do greater things than their parents? I also wonder what even is the status quo? I think it would help to know what is considered to be that because it can make a big difference in the results of this graph. 
A clever title for this would be: The Dwindling Education of Males

raw_comment:
I notice for the graph on the right that in every single country where numbers were recorded more females go on to higher education than boys do. 
 I wonder why women today are still thought of as less educated than men, when these numbers clearly show women get more education. 
  For the graph on the left I notice that countries with a stable economy are at the bottom. Germany and the United states are low in this graph but have good economies. Maybe this graph shows us that education isn't the only factor that benefits economy, or it's simply saying that the parents in these countries received a lot of education. I can also infer that South Korea has gotten more intense with its education over time.
  A catchy headline for the graph on the right could be: "The Numbers Don't Lie, the Girls are Schooling the Boys"
